questions.stem:
Statements: No bird is a fish. All sparrows are birds.
Which conclusion definitely follows?
questions.explanation: The circle of sparrows lies wholly inside the circle of birds, and the bird circle is completely separate from the fish circle. So the sparrow circle cannot touch the fish circle either, and no sparrow is a fish.

optionRationale.1: This contradicts the first statement, which keeps fish and birds apart.
optionRationale.3: The sparrow circle lies inside the bird circle, which does not touch the fish circle.
optionRationale.4: Reversing 'All sparrows are birds' to a universal statement is not valid.

questions.objective: Draw a conclusion from one negative and one universal statement

questions.stem: A boy standing in an open field faces the rising sun. In which direction is his left hand pointing?
questions.explanation: The sun rises in the east, so the boy faces east. With the east in front of him, the north lies on his left side and the south on his right side, while the west is behind him. So his left hand points to the north.

optionRationale.1: South is on his right hand.
optionRationale.3: East is in front of him.
optionRationale.4: West is behind him.

questions.objective: Apply direction sense using the rising sun

questions.stem: The sister of one's father is called the
questions.explanation: The word paternal tells that the relative belongs to the father's side. A father's sister is therefore the paternal aunt, while the sister of the mother would be the maternal aunt. Remember that maternal means the mother side and paternal means the father side.

optionRationale.1: A maternal aunt is the sister of the mother.
optionRationale.2: A niece is the daughter of one's brother or sister.
optionRationale.4: A sister-in-law is the wife of a brother or the sister of a spouse.

questions.objective: Recall blood relation terms

questions.stem: In a class of 30 students, Asha ranks 8th from the top. What is her rank from the bottom?
questions.explanation: Rank from the bottom = total - rank from the top + 1 = 30 - 8 + 1 = 23. Check: 7 students are above Asha and 22 below her, so she is 22 + 1 = 23rd from the bottom. Always count the person once only when you convert a rank from one end to the other end.

optionRationale.1: This is 30 - 8 and forgets to add 1.
optionRationale.2: This subtracts 9 instead of adding 1 to the difference.
optionRationale.3: This adds 2 to the difference instead of 1.

questions.objective: Convert a rank from the top to a rank from the bottom

questions.stem: Today is a Wednesday. Which day of the week will it be after 10 days?
questions.explanation: Ten days is one week and 3 odd days, since 10 = 7 + 3. Counting 3 days forward from Wednesday gives Thursday, Friday, Saturday, so the day is Saturday. Counting odd days is faster than listing every date in between.

optionRationale.2: Friday would be after 9 days.
optionRationale.3: Sunday would be after 11 days.
optionRationale.4: Thursday would be after 8 days.

questions.objective: Use odd days to find a weekday

questions.stem: Four persons stand in a queue. Mohan stands ahead of Sohan, Sohan stands ahead of Rohan, and Rohan stands ahead of Gopal. Who is at the back of the queue?
questions.explanation: The clues give a single chain Mohan, Sohan, Rohan, Gopal from the front. Each person is ahead of the next one, so the last person named, Gopal, is at the back. Write the persons in a line from front to back to see the order clearly.

optionRationale.1: Gopal stands behind Rohan.
optionRationale.3: Both Rohan and Gopal stand behind Sohan.
optionRationale.4: Mohan is at the front of the queue.

questions.objective: Order persons from simple clues

questions.stem: A man walks 7 km west and then 3 km east. How far is he from his starting point, and in which direction?
questions.explanation: The two legs lie along the same line in opposite directions, so subtract: 7 - 3 = 4 km. The larger leg was towards the west, so he is 4 km west of the starting point.

optionRationale.1: This adds the two legs, although they are in opposite directions.
optionRationale.2: His net movement is towards the west, not the east.
optionRationale.4: This ignores the 7 km walked west and the 3 km east does not leave him 3 km away.

questions.objective: Find the net displacement along a line

questions.stem:
Statement: Every member of the chess club is above 18 years of age. Mohan is a member of the chess club.
Which conclusion definitely follows?
options: Mohan plays better than other members
Every person above 18 years is a member of the club
Mohan is above 18 years of age
questions.explanation: Mohan belongs to the group of chess club members, and every member of this group is above 18. So Mohan is above 18. The other choices bring in comparisons or exact values that the statement does not give.

optionRationale.1: Nothing in the statement compares the skill of members.
optionRationale.2: This reverses a universal statement, which is not valid.
optionRationale.3: The statement only says above 18, so the exact age is not known.

questions.objective: Apply a universal statement to a member

questions.stem: P always tells the truth. P says that Q is a liar. Q says that R is a liar. Which of the following is correct?
options: R is a liar on some days only
questions.explanation: P is truthful, so Q is really a liar. Whatever a liar says is false, so Q's statement 'R is a liar' is false, which means R is not a liar. Hence R tells the truth.

optionRationale.2: Q is a liar, so Q's claim that R is a liar is false.
optionRationale.3: Both P's and Q's statements are enough to decide R's type.
optionRationale.4: Each person here is either always truthful or always a liar.

questions.objective: Chain truth-teller statements

questions.stem: The father of one's father is called one's
questions.explanation: Going up one generation through the father gives the father, and going up once more through the father gives his father. That person is the paternal grandfather. Always check the family line the term belongs to before choosing.

optionRationale.1: A maternal grandfather is the father of the mother.
optionRationale.3: A paternal uncle is the brother of the father.
optionRationale.4: A great-grandfather is one generation further back.

questions.objective: Recall blood relation terms

questions.stem: Which statement is a valid reversal of 'Some engineers are artists'?
questions.explanation: A particular affirmative statement can be reversed to another particular affirmative statement, because the overlapping part of the two circles belongs to both. So 'Some engineers are artists' gives 'Some artists are engineers'. Only particular affirmative and universal negative statements can be reversed without changing their kind.

optionRationale.1: A particular statement cannot be turned into a universal one.
optionRationale.2: This contradicts the given statement.
optionRationale.4: This is stronger than what 'some' allows.

questions.objective: Reverse a particular affirmative statement

questions.stem:
Statements: Some doctors are teachers. All teachers are singers.
Which of the following conclusions follow?
A. Some doctors are singers.
B. All doctors are singers.
C. Some singers are teachers.
questions.explanation: The doctors who are teachers lie inside the teachers circle, which lies inside singers, so some doctors are singers (A). Reversing 'All teachers are singers' gives 'Some singers are teachers' (C). B would need every doctor to be a teacher, which is not stated.

optionRationale.1: C also follows, as the converse of 'All teachers are singers' gives 'Some singers are teachers'.
optionRationale.2: B does not follow, since only the doctors who are teachers are known to be singers.
optionRationale.3: B does not follow, so including all three is wrong.

questions.objective: Test conclusions from a universal and a particular statement

questions.stem:
Statements: All pencils are boxes. No box is a ruler.
Conclusions: I. No pencil is a ruler. II. Some pencils are rulers.
Which option is correct?
questions.explanation: The pencil circle is inside the box circle, and the box circle is completely separate from the ruler circle. So the pencil circle is also separate from the ruler circle, giving I. II says the opposite, so it cannot follow.

optionRationale.2: II contradicts the premises, because the pencil circle lies inside the box circle that is apart from rulers.
optionRationale.3: I and II contradict each other, so both cannot follow.
optionRationale.4: I follows directly from the two statements.

questions.objective: Combine a universal affirmative with a universal negative

questions.stem: Facing north, a man walks 10 m, turns right and walks 4 m, turns right again and walks 10 m, then turns left and walks 3 m. How far is he from the starting point and in which direction?
questions.explanation: Going 10 m north then turning right gives 4 m east. A second right turn faces south, so he returns 10 m south to the starting latitude. Facing south, a left turn points east, so he goes 3 m east. He is 4 + 3 = 7 m east of the start.

optionRationale.1: He moved east first, so he cannot end up west of the start.
optionRationale.3: This adds 10 and 3, but the two 10 m legs cancel each other.
optionRationale.4: The last leg goes east, not south, and the earlier 4 m east is also part of the displacement.

questions.objective: Track a path with several turns

questions.stem: A is the sister of B. C is the mother of B. D is the father of C. How is A related to D?
questions.explanation: A and B are children of C, because B is C's child and A is B's sister. D is the father of C, so D is the grandfather of A. As A is female, she is D's granddaughter.

optionRationale.1: D is the father of C, who is A's mother, not of A.
optionRationale.2: A niece would be the daughter of a brother or sister of D.
optionRationale.4: That needs one more generation between A and D.

questions.objective: Resolve a blood relation chain

questions.stem: In a class of 45 students, Rina ranks 12th from the top and Sana is 9 places below Rina. What is Sana's rank from the bottom?
questions.explanation: Sana's rank from the top is 12 + 9 = 21. Her rank from the bottom is 45 - 21 + 1 = 25. Check: 20 students are above her and 24 below, and 24 + 1 = 25. Remember to add one when you convert a rank from one end to the other end.

optionRationale.1: This is 45 - 21 and forgets to add 1.
optionRationale.2: This adds one too many to the correct result.
optionRationale.3: This is 45 - 12, which ignores the 9 places below Rina.

questions.objective: Combine rank changes with total strength

questions.stem: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a round table facing the centre. Clockwise means clockwise as seen from above. B sits immediately clockwise of A. D sits opposite A. C sits opposite B. E sits immediately anticlockwise of D. Who sits opposite E?
questions.explanation: Number the seats 1 to 6 clockwise with A in seat 1. Then B is in seat 2, D in seat 4 and C in seat 5. E is anticlockwise of D, so E is in seat 3, leaving F in seat 6, which is opposite seat 3.

optionRationale.2: A sits opposite D, not E.
optionRationale.3: C sits opposite B, not E.
optionRationale.4: B sits opposite C, not E.

questions.objective: Solve a six-person circular arrangement

questions.stem: If 1 March of a certain year is a Monday, which day of the week is 1 April of the same year?
questions.explanation: March has 31 days, and 31 = 4 x 7 + 3, so there are 3 odd days. Counting 3 days forward from Monday gives Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. So 1 April is a Thursday. Month lengths of 28, 29, 30 and 31 days leave 0, 1, 2 and 3 odd days respectively.

optionRationale.1: This counts only 2 odd days.
optionRationale.3: This counts 4 odd days.
optionRationale.4: This counts only 1 odd day.

questions.objective: Find a weekday one month later

questions.stem: In a leap year, 10 February is a Thursday. Which day is 10 March of that year?
questions.explanation: In a leap year February has 29 days, so 10 March is 29 days after 10 February. Since 29 = 4 x 7 + 1, there is 1 odd day. One day after Thursday is Friday.

optionRationale.1: This would hold if February had 28 days.
optionRationale.2: This counts 2 odd days, but only 1 is left over.
optionRationale.4: This moves backwards instead of forwards.

questions.objective: Handle a leap-year February in weekday questions

questions.stem:
Advertisement: 'Drink milk daily to build strong bones.'
Which of the following assumptions is implicit?
I. Milk contains substances that help bone growth.
II. Nobody can have strong bones without drinking milk.
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
questions.explanation: The advice makes sense only if milk helps bones, so I is assumed. II is an extreme claim using 'nobody', and an advertisement recommending milk does not need to deny every other source of strong bones. Hence only I is implicit.

optionRationale.1: The advice does not say milk is the only way to get strong bones.
optionRationale.2: II is too strong to be taken for granted.
optionRationale.3: I must be taken for granted, otherwise the advice has no point.

questions.objective: Identify an implicit assumption in an advertisement

questions.stem:
Should homework be banned for primary school children?
Argument I: Yes, because long homework leaves young children little time to play and rest, which they need to grow.
Argument II: No, because my neighbour's child does homework every day and is happy.
Which argument is strong?
options: Both I and II are strong
Neither I nor II is strong
questions.explanation: Argument I gives a relevant, general reason connected to the issue: time for play and rest. Argument II rests on one personal example and does not address why homework should or should not be banned, so it is weak.

optionRationale.2: II relies on a single example, which is a weak basis.
optionRationale.3: II is weak since one case proves nothing about children in general.
optionRationale.4: I gives a relevant reason linked to the welfare of children.

questions.objective: Judge the strength of arguments

questions.stem:
Problem: Many fields in a village are flooded every monsoon because the main drain is choked with silt.
Courses of action: I. The village council should clear and widen the drain before the next monsoon. II. All farmers should be told to give up farming in the village.
Which follows?
questions.explanation: The flooding is caused by a choked drain, so clearing and widening it addresses the cause and is practical. Asking all farmers to give up farming punishes the victims and leaves the real problem untouched.

optionRationale.1: Giving up farming is extreme and does not remove the cause of flooding.
optionRationale.3: II is impractical, so it does not follow.
optionRationale.4: I is a practical step that addresses the cause.

questions.objective: Choose a practical course of action

questions.stem:
Statements: All cats are mammals. All mammals are animals. Some animals are pets.
Which of the following conclusions follow?
A. All cats are animals.
B. Some pets are animals.
C. Some cats are pets.
questions.explanation: The cat circle is inside mammals, which is inside animals, so A follows. 'Some animals are pets' reverses to 'Some pets are animals', so B follows. The pets may be animals that are not cats, so C is not forced.

optionRationale.1: B also follows, since the converse of 'Some animals are pets' is valid.
optionRationale.2: C does not follow, as the pets may be animals other than cats.
optionRationale.4: A follows from the two universal statements, so it must be included.

questions.objective: Test conclusions in a chain of statements

questions.stem: Match List-I (facing direction and turn) with List-II (new direction).
questions.explanation: A right turn from west points north (I). A left turn from south points east (II). A right turn from east points south (III). A left turn from north points west (IV). Hence A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV.

optionRationale.1: A and B are swapped; a right turn from west gives north, not east.
optionRationale.2: C and D are swapped; a right turn from east gives south.
optionRationale.3: Every pair is reversed, which gives the directions after turns of 180 degrees.

questions.objective: Match turns with the resulting directions

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In a row, if X is 10th from the left end and 10th from the right end, the row has 19 persons.
Reason (R): The total number of persons is the sum of the two positions minus one.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: X is counted from both ends, so the total is 10 + 10 - 1 = 19. R states the rule used and explains why the answer is 19 and not 20. Check: 9 persons are on each side of X, and 9 + 1 + 9 = 19.

optionRationale.2: R is the correct explanation of A, not just a true statement.
optionRationale.3: R is true, so (A) is true but (R) is false cannot hold.
optionRationale.4: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Apply the sum-minus-one rule for a row

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): From the statement 'No pen is a book' it follows that 'Some pens are books'.
Reason (R): 'No A is B' means that the circles of A and B do not overlap.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A is false because a negative statement keeps the circles apart, so no pen can be a book. R is true, since 'No A is B' means separate circles. Hence A is false and R is true.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so options 1, 2 and 3 are wrong.
optionRationale.2: A is false, so options 1, 2 and 3 are wrong.
optionRationale.3: R is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Understand what a universal negative statement means

questions.stem: Kavita's mother is the sister of my father. How is Kavita related to me?
questions.explanation: Kavita's mother is my father's sister, i.e. my paternal aunt. The child of my aunt is my cousin. Kavita and I do not share both parents, so she is not my sister. Write the relations as a short family tree to avoid confusing generations.

optionRationale.2: A niece would be the daughter of my brother or sister.
optionRationale.3: A sister would have the same parents as I do.
optionRationale.4: An aunt would be the sister of one of my parents.

questions.objective: Resolve a relation through an aunt

questions.stem: Early in the morning, Ravi stands in an open field with his shadow falling to his right. Which direction is he facing?
questions.explanation: The sun rises in the east, so a morning shadow falls towards the west. If the shadow lies on Ravi's right, then the west is on his right. A person facing south has west on the right, so Ravi faces south.

optionRationale.1: Facing north, his right is east, but the morning shadow falls towards the west.
optionRationale.2: Facing east, the shadow would fall behind him.
optionRationale.3: Facing west, the shadow would fall in front of him.

questions.objective: Use the sun and shadow to find direction

questions.stem: Meera walks 20 m south, turns left and walks 5 m, then turns left again and walks 8 m. How far is she from the starting point and in which direction?
questions.explanation: Facing south, a left turn points east, so she goes 5 m east. A second left turn points north, so she goes 8 m north. Net: 5 m east and 20 - 8 = 12 m south. The distance is the square root of 25 + 144 = 13 m, to the south-east.

optionRationale.2: She ends up 12 m south of the start, so she is not north of it.
optionRationale.3: This adds 12 and 5 instead of using Pythagoras theorem.
optionRationale.4: Her left turn from south goes east, so she ends up east, not west.

questions.objective: Find the final displacement after two left turns

questions.stem: Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F sit in a row facing north. A is at the right end. C sits third from the left. D does not sit next to C. E sits immediately to the left of F. B sits somewhere to the left of C. Who sits at the left end?
questions.explanation: A is sixth and C is third. E and F, adjacent with E on the left, can only take the fourth and fifth seats. That leaves seats 1 and 2 for B and D. D cannot be next to C, so D is first and B second. The order is D, B, C, E, F, A.

optionRationale.1: B must be second, since D cannot be next to C and fills the first seat.
optionRationale.3: E and F take the fourth and fifth seats.
optionRationale.4: F is fifth from the left, immediately right of E.

questions.objective: Solve a six-person row arrangement

questions.stem: Eight persons A to H sit around a round table facing the centre. Clockwise means clockwise as seen from above. B sits immediately clockwise of A. E sits opposite A. G sits opposite B. C sits immediately clockwise of G. H sits opposite C. F sits immediately anticlockwise of A. Who are the two neighbours of G?
questions.explanation: Put A in seat 1 and number clockwise. B is seat 2, E seat 5, G seat 6, C seat 7, H seat 3 (opposite C) and F seat 8. D takes seat 4. Seat 6 holds G, with E in seat 5 and C in seat 7 as neighbours.

optionRationale.1: D sits next to E on the other side, not next to G.
optionRationale.2: F is next to A and C, not next to G.
optionRationale.4: H and D sit on the other side of the table from G.

questions.objective: Solve an eight-person circular arrangement

questions.stem: A says 'B and C are both liars'. B says 'A is a liar'. C says 'A and B are of different types (one truthful, the other a liar)'. Each person is either always truthful or always a liar. Who are truthful?
questions.explanation: Suppose A is truthful. Then B and C are liars, but C says that A and B are of different types, which would be true, and a liar cannot say that. So A is a liar. Then B's claim 'A is a liar' is true, so B is truthful, and C's claim about A and B is true, so C is truthful.

optionRationale.1: If A were truthful, B and C would be liars, but C's claim that A and B differ would then be true, which a liar cannot say.
optionRationale.2: If A is truthful then C is a liar, so A and C cannot both be truthful.
optionRationale.3: If B is truthful then A is a liar, and C's claim that A and B differ is then true, so C must also be truthful.

questions.objective: Solve a three-person truth-teller puzzle

questions.stem: A month of 31 days has exactly five Fridays, five Saturdays and five Sundays. On which day of the week does the month begin?
questions.explanation: A 31-day month has four full weeks plus 3 extra days, and those extra days are the first three days of the month. They occur five times, so the first three days must be Friday, Saturday and Sunday. The month therefore begins on Friday.

optionRationale.2: Then the five repeated days would be Thursday, Friday and Saturday.
optionRationale.3: Then the five repeated days would be Saturday, Sunday and Monday.
optionRationale.4: Then the five repeated days would be Sunday, Monday and Tuesday.

questions.objective: Deduce the first day of a month from repeated weekdays

questions.stem: If 15 August 2027 is a Sunday, on which day of the week did 15 August 2025 fall?
questions.explanation: From 15 August 2025 to 15 August 2027 there are two years, and no 29 February falls in between, so 365 + 365 = 730 days. Since 730 = 104 x 7 + 2, the later date is 2 days after the earlier date. Two days before Sunday is Friday.

optionRationale.1: This counts only 1 odd day backwards.
optionRationale.3: This counts 3 odd days backwards.
optionRationale.4: This moves forward instead of backward.

questions.objective: Move back through years to find a weekday

questions.stem: In a queue, Neha is 7th from the front and Priya is 12th from the back. After they exchange places, Neha becomes 18th from the front. How many persons are in the queue?
questions.explanation: After the exchange Neha is in Priya's old place, so Priya was 18th from the front. She was also 12th from the back, so the total is 18 + 12 - 1 = 29. Neha's original place, 7th from the front, does not change this total.

optionRationale.1: This is 18 + 12 and forgets to subtract 1.
optionRationale.2: This subtracts 2 instead of 1.
optionRationale.4: This is Priya's original position from the front, not the total.

questions.objective: Use an exchange of positions to find the total

questions.stem: Five friends A, B, C, D and E have different heights. A is taller than B. C is shorter than B. D is taller than A. E is shorter than C. Who is the third tallest?
questions.explanation: The clues combine to D > A > B > C > E. Counting from the tallest, D is first, A second, B third, C fourth and E fifth. So B is the third tallest. Positive and negative displacements along the same line should always be added with their signs.

optionRationale.1: A is the second tallest.
optionRationale.2: C is the fourth tallest.
optionRationale.3: D is the tallest.

questions.objective: Order persons by height from comparisons

questions.stem: Starting from a point P, Kiran walks 15 m west, turns right and walks 12 m, turns right again and walks 15 m, then turns left and walks 4 m. How far and in which direction is he from P?
questions.explanation: Facing west, a right turn points north, so he goes 12 m north. Another right turn points east, and 15 m east cancels the 15 m west. Facing east, a left turn points north, so he goes 4 m more north. He is 12 + 4 = 16 m north of P.

optionRationale.2: This counts only the last leg and ignores the 12 m walked north.
optionRationale.3: The 15 m west and 15 m east cancel, so he has no east-west displacement.
optionRationale.4: This leaves out the final 4 m walked north.

questions.objective: Track a path with cancelling legs

questions.stem:
Statements: Some artists are bakers. No baker is a cyclist. All cyclists are dancers.
Which of the following conclusions follow?
A. Some artists are not cyclists.
B. No cyclist is a baker.
C. Some dancers are bakers.
questions.explanation: The artists who are bakers cannot be cyclists, so some artists are not cyclists (A). 'No baker is a cyclist' reverses to 'No cyclist is a baker' (B). The bakers may be completely outside the circle of dancers, so C is not forced.

optionRationale.1: B also follows, because 'No baker is a cyclist' can be reversed.
optionRationale.3: A follows too, and C does not follow.
optionRationale.4: C does not follow, as bakers may lie wholly outside dancers.

questions.objective: Test conclusions from three linked statements

questions.stem:
Statements: All students are readers. Some readers are writers. No writer is a poet.
Which of the following conclusions follow?
A. Some readers are not poets.
B. No student is a poet.
C. Some writers are readers.
questions.explanation: The readers who are writers are not poets, so some readers are not poets (A). 'Some readers are writers' reverses to 'Some writers are readers' (C). Students lie inside readers, and the readers may include poets, so B is not forced.

optionRationale.1: B does not follow, because some students could be poets who are not writers.
optionRationale.2: A also follows, and B does not.
optionRationale.4: B does not follow, as readers may include poets.

questions.objective: Test conclusions from three linked statements

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Two particular statements, such as 'Some A are B' and 'Some B are C', never give a definite conclusion.
Reason (R): Any such pair of statements forces the circles of A and C to be separate.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A is true because the A and C circles may overlap, touch different parts of B or stay apart, so nothing definite follows. R is false, since the circles are not forced apart. Hence A is true and R is false.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so options 1 and 2 are wrong.
optionRationale.2: R is false, so options 1 and 2 are wrong.
optionRationale.4: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Know why two particular statements give no conclusion

questions.stem: Four persons A, B, C and D are each either always truthful or always lying. A says 'Exactly one of B, C and D is truthful'. B says 'A is a liar'. C says 'B and D are of the same type'. D says 'Exactly two of the four of us are liars'. Who are truthful?
questions.explanation: Take A as truthful: exactly one of B, C, D is truthful. B says A is a liar, so B lies. If C were truthful, D would be a liar like B, giving exactly two liars and making D's claim true, a contradiction. So D is truthful, C lies, and the two liars B and C fit D's claim.

optionRationale.2: Then D would be truthful too, leaving only A as a liar, so D's claim of exactly two liars would be false.
optionRationale.3: Then B and D would both be liars, which makes exactly two liars and so D's claim would be true, a contradiction.
optionRationale.4: Then A, B and C would be three liars, so D's claim of exactly two liars would be false.

questions.objective: Solve a four-person truth-teller puzzle

questions.stem:
A notice in a reading hall says: 'Do not use mobile phones here.'
Which assumptions are implicit?
I. Mobile phone use can disturb the readers in the hall.
II. Readers will read the notice and many will follow it.
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
questions.explanation: The notice is put up because phone use is believed to harm the hall, which is assumption I. It is also put up in the hope that readers will see it and obey it, which is II. Both are taken for granted, so both are implicit.

optionRationale.1: II is also taken for granted, otherwise a notice would be pointless.
optionRationale.3: I is also taken for granted, since this is why phones are not wanted.
optionRationale.4: Both are needed for the notice to make sense.

questions.objective: Identify implicit assumptions behind a notice

questions.stem: In a non-leap year, 1 January is a Monday. On which day of the week does 1 March fall?
questions.explanation: January has 31 days and February has 28 in a non-leap year, so 1 March is 59 days after 1 January. Since 59 = 8 x 7 + 3, there are 3 odd days. Three days after Monday is Thursday.

optionRationale.1: This counts only 2 odd days.
optionRationale.2: This counts 4 odd days.
optionRationale.4: This counts 1 odd day.

questions.objective: Count odd days across two months

questions.stem: Five persons P, Q, R, S and T live on different floors of a five-storey building, numbered 1 (lowest) to 5 (top). P does not live on the top or the bottom floor. Q lives two floors above R. S and T live on adjacent floors. T lives above P. S does not live on the top floor. Who lives on the fourth floor?
questions.explanation: The pair (R, Q) can be on floors (1, 3), (2, 4) or (3, 5). Testing (2, 4) leaves floors 1 and 5 for S and T, which are not adjacent, and (3, 5) leaves no valid place for P, S and T. With (1, 3), P is on floor 2, T on 5 and S on 4.

optionRationale.1: T lives on the top floor.
optionRationale.2: Q lives on the third floor.
optionRationale.3: P lives on the second floor.

questions.objective: Solve a floor allocation puzzle

questions.stem: P is the brother of Q. Q is the daughter of R. R is the wife of S. T is the father of S. How is T related to P?
questions.explanation: Q is a child of R and S, and P is Q's brother, so P is also their child. S is therefore P's father. T is the father of S, which makes T the father of P's father, that is, the paternal grandfather.

optionRationale.2: T is the father of S, who is P's father, not of R.
optionRationale.3: S is the father of P; T is one generation above.
optionRationale.4: A paternal uncle would be a brother of S, not his father.

questions.objective: Resolve a longer blood relation chain
